title: Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts
claim: Existing models occupy a narrow corner of a design space; widening both axes opens a feasible region balancing human and task constraints.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, 2-D plane map then constraint curves
description: Two panels share the axis label 'Functional form'. The left panel is a 2-D map. The y-axis is 'Number of Experts', running from 1 to infinity. The x-axis runs from Simple Boolean through Linear and User-defined subspace to Over-parameterized MLP. Colored regions mark existing model families. A yellow triangle at the lower left holds CMR, LEN and CBM and is labeled SIMPLE. A purple band across the top holds DCR, LICEM and SENN and is labeled INTRACTABLE INTERPRETABILITY. A tall red strip at the right is labeled KNOTTY. A large green 'UNCHARTED RESEARCH AREA' in the middle holds the red labels Lin-M-CBE and Sym-M-CBE, the new proposals. The right panel is a schematic. A green curve (task constraints) and a red curve (human constraints) bound a white feasible region. The rest is hatched. A dashed red curve and two small scientist and student icons mark the human viewpoint.
caption: Left: The plane defined by functional form and number of experts. Different CBMs occupy distinct positions in this space, with regions highlighted in different colors. We indicate our newly proposed instantiations in red. Right: The red curve denotes human constraints, and the green curve denotes task constraints. The region bounded by the two curves represents the set of feasible models.
abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) promote interpretability by grounding predictions in human-understandable concepts. However, existing CBMs typically constrain their task predictor to a single expression whose functional form is set a priori, limiting both predictive accuracy and adaptability to diverse user needs. We propose Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts (M-CBE), a framework that generalizes existing CBMs along two dimensions: the number of expressions, referred to as experts, employed by the task predictor to map concepts to the task, and the functional form each expression takes, thus exposing an underexplored region of this design space. We investigate this region by instantiating two novel models: Linear M-CBE, which learns a finite set of linear expressions, and Symbolic M-CBE, which leverages symbolic regression to discover expert functions from data subject to user-specified operator vocabularies. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that varying the number of expressions and their functional form provides a robust framework for navigating the accuracy-interpretability trade-off.
